understanding the evolution of host-parasite interactions and how the spatial variation in the prevalence of parasites affects the evolution of the major histocompatibility (MHC) genes of a host species.

the MHC of this bird is shaped by the environment, but the exact nature of this relationship is not yet clear.
MHC diversity and composition are associated with haemosporidian infections in a spatially variable fashion, and that the environment may shape MHC-parasitism relationships in passerines.

we found evidence of negative frequency-dependent MHC-parasitism associations in rufous-capped sparrows (Z. capensis) across the Andes of Peru, which suggests that the environment can influence the evolution of host–parasitism interactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the MHC of hosts is not static, but is shaped by the local environment, which in turn shapes the diversity and composition patterns of MHC alleles.
the environment can shape the evolution of the MHC, and this can be studied by comparing populations with contrasting environmental conditions and parasite pressure.

the environment shapes host–pathogen interactions, and that the spatial distribution of parasites and their impact on the host immune system is a major determinant of host genetic diversity and the evolution of host defense genes.
